commit.message:
ci: state when each route's version bumps, and fail a release that leaves one stale (#144)

* docs(release-installer): state when to bump each route's version

The installer and every route keep their own version, but nothing said when
a route's version should move. A route whose agent updates by version
(Claude Code, Pi) delivers nothing until it is bumped, while routes that
track main use the string only as telemetry. The skill now has a rule per
case and a check for stale routes, and a latest release carries the
confirmed route bumps. AGENTS.md no longer says a release leaves every
other route alone, which the 0.5.0 release already contradicted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ci: fail a release PR that leaves a route's version stale

People releasing by hand had only prose to tell them which routes to bump.
scripts/route-versions.js now applies the rule: it lists each route with
changes since its last version change (shared content for routes whose
agent updates by version, the route's own files for every route), proposes
a version from the conventional-commit prefixes, and --write sets every
string a route's bump moves. The new Route versions job runs it on any pull
request that moves a version, so a release can't leave a route behind.
scripts/routes.js records how each agent updates and which files each
route owns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(route-versions): compare version values, and own every file a manifest names

A route's last version change was the newest commit touching a line with
"version", so reformatting that line hid earlier unreleased changes. It is
now the newest commit whose version value differs from its parent's, and
the release gate compares values too. A route now also owns every file its
manifest names outside the shared content, such as Antigravity's logo and
Codex's apps file, instead of a hand-kept list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(route-versions): refuse a version override that doesn't move forward

`--write claude-code=2.1.0` wrote an older version, which would reset the
route's baseline and reuse a version an agent may still have cached. An
override must now be above the route's current version, checked before
any file is written. The skill also passes the versions the user confirmed
to --write, which otherwise uses its own proposals.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(route-versions): fail a release that moves a route's version back

A hand-edited downgrade counted as a version change, so it reset the
route's baseline and passed --check, while --write refuses the same
downgrade. With --base, a route whose version is lower than at the base
now fails the check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
feat(skills): replace bootstrap with workspaces and cli-install (#141)

* feat(skills): replace bootstrap with workspaces and cli-install

bootstrap mixed four concerns: installing the CLI, signing in, workspace
binding and sync, and plan limits. Split it by owner:

- workspaces: the workspace as the place where a service's API work and
  its context live. Ownership vs. dependency, sharing safely, reading what
  initialization did, and claiming guest work when a plan limit is hit.
  Written as the value of each practice rather than exact commands.
- cli-install: installing and updating the CLI through the route that put
  it there, the MCP fallback, and finding flags with -h.
- api-engineer gains the Sign-in and "Reporting CLI and skill gaps"
  sections that other skills pointed at in bootstrap.

Every bare-name and postman:<name> reference to bootstrap now points at
the skill that owns that concern. manifest.json and the generated
session-start copies are regenerated.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(skills): address review on workspaces, cli-install and references

- Drop workspaces from the session-start hooks; it isn't a core entry.
- workspaces: initialization is the starting point; remove the points on
  working locally, sharing safely and one place of work per service.
- cli-install: one file, with the install, update and uninstall steps
  inlined instead of a separate reference.
- api-engineer: remove the Sign-in section and the references to
  workspaces; describe postman status as the way to see what setup is
  missing; describe a collection as the contract that the CLI's
  deterministic tools turn into a spec, mock, SDK or performance suite.
- api-discovery, api-documentation, api-testing, api-monitoring, flows,
  variables, webhook-testing, datasets and postman-mcp-server no longer
  point at another skill for sign-in or workspace sync; they say sign in,
  or that datasets push with the workspace.

* fix(api-engineer): keep the diff to what removing bootstrap requires

* fix(workspaces, cli-install): name postman init and status; drop uninstall

commit.message:
The simulation context document, as a YAML record (#134)

* docs(api-simulation): make the context document a record the next session parses

The reference described the file as prose that nothing parses, with no
schema to satisfy. That is what made it cheap to write and useless to read
back: a claim carried no status, so a reader could not tell what a run
established from what someone reasoned, there was no way to say a claim had
gone stale, and each session chose its own headings.

It is now a record. Purpose and Execution stay prose and stay the only text
editable outside the markers; prerequisites, assumptions, observations,
didnt-work and fingerprints are YAML lists inside `begin:`/`end:` markers.
Each assumption carries kind, type, status, source, depends_on and affects,
so it is pinned to the fingerprint its evidence was taken against, and the
write-back order is spelled out: fingerprint, staleness pass, sort what you
learned, then statuses. Observations and failures append only, and a
reasoned claim can never read as confirmed.

SKILL.md's section on the document follows, and says to read it first and
write the run back before finishing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): make the context document a YAML file

The record used `<!-- begin:x -->` / `<!-- end:x -->` markers inside a
markdown document, so reading one back meant a regex per section and a
parser that only the convention held together. Five of the seven sections
were already YAML lists; the markers existed only because markdown has no
other way to say "this part is data".

It is now `<name>.context.yaml`: one YAML document under
`schema: simulation-context/v1`, where the key is the boundary. `purpose`

exercised faster than real time and as often as it takes, with none of what a

simulation holds across the worlds explored. That bound is why it is worth

commit.message:
Simulation proxy mode, and a context document that replaces work (#118)

* docs(api-simulation): proxy mode and the simulation context document

Two things the skill doesn't cover yet, both shipped since it was last
written.

`simulation run --proxy` puts the members behind a local forward proxy
that answers for the dependencies' own hostnames, so code reaches its
mocks through HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY with the base URLs it ships with.
"Running it" mentioned the flag in one line; a section now says when to
reach for it (hard-coded hostnames, URLs built from config the change
shouldn't touch, an SDK that owns its base URL, a host that doesn't
resolve) and what it needs: `origin` declared in the mock's own manifest
and carried onto every member built from it, `--doctor` before trusting a
client to honor the variables, all three banner exports in the shell that
starts the code, and the mocked/passed-through log. `reference/
sim_yaml_schema.md` carries the contract — origin matching and stripping,
header forwarding, 502/504, every `--proxy-*` flag and exit code.

Every simulation is now created with a `<name>.context.md` beside it,
holding what running it has taught: the commands that start it and prove
it is up, the preconditions and what breaks when one fails, and what a
passing run still doesn't prove. A new section says to read it before
rebuilding what it answers and to leave it truer, and
`reference/context_file.md` describes its sections, the `@todo` comments
standing in for what needs a real run, and the assumptions it ships with.

Checked against postman-cli `channel/beta` (535ac6a20, which moved
`--proxy` onto the `.sim.yaml` and `origin` onto the mock) and
postman-app (63b5284edf2, which made the context file Markdown), and run
against the eval world's orders service and its five dependency mocks:
`--doctor` reports global fetch ignoring the proxy variables, `POST
/orders` returns 201 with all five hostnames intercepted and
`src/index.ts` unedited, and `--scenario bad-gateway` fails payments
alone while members without that scenario serve their defaults. `--proxy`
is in no stable release yet, so the skill names no minimum version for it
and README is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): stop a simulation by a pattern that matches the run

`pkill -f` matches against the whole command line, so a pattern built from the
bare filename misses a simulation launched by path — which is how the example
above it launches one. The skill now shows a pattern that tolerates the
directory, and says why the obvious one does not work.

manifest.json regenerated via scripts/build-manifest.js.

Mirrors the same fix in postman-app and postman-cli, which generate a context
document carrying this command.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): say what the context document should hold

A real run against a 10-dependency service produced a 150-line context
document: a YAML file with an invented `schema:` key, an inventory of every
route, request shape, valid action, auth mode, mock host and config flag,
per-endpoint call counts and coverage to two decimals. Everything in it that
only the run could know — a Redis setting without which aggregation never
flushes, a stale-key crash and the handler that has no try/catch, a 500 where
a 400 belongs — was buried in material the repo already states.

The skill asked for four sections and said not to restate the simulation
definition, which wasn't enough to decide what each line should be. It now
gives the test the document is written against: the repo doesn't already
state it. What passes is a precondition you had to discover, a failure and
its cause, what the simulation can't reproduce, and which members served or
stayed silent. For routes, request shapes, auth and config it says to name
the file that holds them, which keeps one source true and a credential out of
a committed document, and to write what holds between runs rather than counts
and timings the next run invalidates.

`reference/context_file.md` gains "What earns a line" and an example of a
three-line `## Observations`, and its guidance and rules are phrased as the
action to take throughout, as is the CA-export bullet in the proxy section.
Guidance written as a prohibition leaves an agent a checklist of forbidden
things and no way to judge the case the list didn't name.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): keep failures, and their evidence, across runs

The context document kept only the last run, so a failure recorded in
`## Observations` was gone after the next one — the thing a session least
wants to debug twice. Add `## What didn't work`: the one section that
accretes, a dated line per failure carrying the signature the next session
recognizes it by, capped at the ten most recent.

Claims now carry their evidence too. The log they came from isn't committed,
so each one in `## Assumptions` and `## What didn't work` is dated and says
whether a run established it or someone reasoned it out, and "Working with
it" says what that buys a reader: an observed claim holds until a run
contradicts it, a reasoned one is a hypothesis worth checking. Evidence beyond
the line goes by reference — the handler that threw, the mock example, the
test that reproduces it — never the run's log, which isn't committed and the
next run overwrites.

In the skill: point at the document where an existing simulation is first
mentioned, since reading it there is what saves rebuilding the commands and
preconditions, and write the run back from "Before you say it works", the
checklist a run actually reaches. Its section drops the guidance the
reference already carries.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): drop invented paths from the pointer rule

`config/actions.js` and `config/env/development.js` read as conventions a
repo is expected to have, and neither is one. The examples were only there
to show the shape of a pointer, which the generated `## Purpose` already
demonstrates by naming the handlers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): leave the CLI's flags to the CLI's own help

The `--proxy` flag table in reference/sim_yaml_schema.md restated what
`postman simulation run --help` already says, and half of what it added
was behaviour the help ought to state itself. A table in two places
drifts the next time only one is edited, so this drops it for a pointer
at `--help`, and the gaps it was covering are being filled in the CLI
instead (--port's fallback, --proxy-port's binding, --scenario's default,
--log-format's fields, the 504/502 and exit-2 rules).

The same reasoning removes the proxy internals from the schema
reference, the stop-signal mechanics and 127.0.0.1 note from SKILL.md,
and the enumerated generated assumptions from the context-file
reference. `--port` goes back to being optional, with the `listening`
event named as where the bound port and member addresses come from, so
nothing depends on the port that was asked for.

Also records bringing a mock in as a dependency before building the
simulation over it, and what a run takes for granted about a
dependency's own behaviour as something the context document holds.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): answer the review on the proxy and the context document

Name the three shell environment variables where the skill asks for
them, rather than calling them "the variables" a section after the
paragraph that introduced them, and say why they belong to the shell
that starts the service: they are read by the HTTP client inside it, not
by the CLI, which is the proxy's destination rather than its client.

Say where the proxy logs — its own stdout, the terminal it was started
in — which the previous wording left to inference.

`## Observations` now accretes a dated line per run, newest first,
keeping the five most recent, instead of being replaced each time. A
member silent across three consecutive runs is a pattern; the same fact
seen once is not, and the section's value was being thrown away every
run. It stays bounded so the file keeps to a screenful, the way
`## What didn't work` keeps its ten. The CLI's generated template is
being changed to match.

State what the context document already answers rather than instructing
a reader not to rebuild it. The guidance is the same — `## Execution`'s
commands ran and `## Assumptions`'s preconditions were established, so
both are usable as they stand — without the prescription.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): leave proxy mechanics to the CLI's help

The skill told the agent which environment variables to export, in which
shell, and how to preload an undici dispatcher around Node's fetch. None
of that is a judgement the skill is for, and all of it moves with the
CLI: the variables, the per-run CA and the per-client fixes are printed
by `simulation run --proxy` itself and by `--doctor`, so a copy here can
only go stale or disagree.

What the skill keeps is what the command can't say for itself: that
proxy mode is the answer when no base URL can change, and the two things
that decide whether a proxied run proved anything — `origin:` belonging
to the mock rather than the .sim.yaml, so a member without one silently
reaches the real service, and conditions not applying, so an injected
failure needs the one-port run. For the rest it points at
`postman simulation run --help` and lets the agent read the CLI it
actually has.

This also drops the NODE_OPTIONS line whose quoting was under review;
the non-invasive preload now lives in the CLI's own --doctor output,
where it is next to the problem it solves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): a proxied run matches on the member's origin, not the mock's

Both files can carry `origin:`, and the run reads the one in the
`.sim.yaml`. `proxy/config.js` normalizes `rawMock.origin` — "a raw
mocks[] entry as written in YAML" — and its header says so outright: the
proxied run loads the same `.sim.yaml` "read here for hostname routing".
The mock's manifest is where the value is *declared*; `simulation create`
copies it onto each member as it writes the file.

The skill and the schema reference both had it the other way round, and
the reference went further, saying every simulation using a mock
intercepts the same hosts — which reads as a live link when it is a copy
taken once. The consequence is the part worth knowing either way: adding
an `origin:` to a manifest leaves an existing `.sim.yaml` alone until the
member is edited or the simulation recreated, and a member's `origin:`
can be edited on its own, which is how one mock stands in for different
hosts in two simulations.

The reference now shows both files, and records that two members
claiming one hostname fails the run rather than picking a winner.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): tighten the origin rule

Two YAML blocks and four paragraphs for one fact, with the
silent-passthrough consequence stated twice. Same content, half the
lines.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(api-simulation): keep the schema reference to the schema

Proxy mode isn't a `.sim.yaml` field, and the skill already says what the
proxy does with a request and which flags to take from the CLI's own help.
What belongs here is `origin` itself, so the section is now that field:
where its value comes from, how a scheme and port are stripped, what an
unmatchable value and a collision do, and why a mock declaring none leaves
the key out. The rule that `--proxy` takes no simulation id joins the
existing by-path rule instead of standing alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(installer): auto-approve Postman's Codex hook (#124)

* fix(codex): pin the marketplace to codex-release, so hook approval survives updates

Codex 0.164 binds a plugin hook's approval to a hash of every file under
the plugin, and refetches git marketplaces when it starts. Our marketplace
tracked main, and the cached plugin holds the snapshot's .git and its
revision, so every commit to main made Codex ask again to approve the
session-start hook, and the mandate was missing until the user did.

Codex users now track codex-release, which moves only on a Codex route
release:

- codex-release.yml fast-forwards the branch to the newest commit on main
  that changed .codex-plugin/plugin.json's version, never backwards.
- The installer adds the marketplace with --ref codex-release and upgrades
  it at once, since `add` records no revision and Codex would refetch at
  its next start. It reads the ref from $CODEX_HOME/config.toml, re-adds a
  marketplace registered with no ref, and refuses one at another ref.
- Installer smoke checks the real Codex records the ref.
- README's Codex commands take the ref; CONTRIBUTING says why.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(codex): build the config path with path.join, as the installer does

On Windows the installer reads \home\user\.codex\config.toml, so fixtures
keyed by a POSIX path were never found and every ref check fell through.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(codex): fail closed on a ref the installer can't read, and release from first-parent history

marketplaceRef read a quoted key, a multi-line string or an escaped
string as "no ref", so the installer would remove an explicitly pinned
marketplace and re-add it at codex-release. Any ref line it can't parse
now returns undefined, and the install stops with the remove command.

codex-release.yml walked path-limited history, which follows a merge
commit's PR side and picks the PR's bump commit, missing what main
gained since the PR branched. It now walks first-parent history, so the
merge commit is the release.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(codex): keep Postman installed when moving a marketplace to codex-release fails

`codex plugin marketplace remove` uninstalls the plugin too, so a failed
add, upgrade or plugin add after it left the user with no Postman. The
migration now checks codex-release is reachable before removing
anything, and a failure after the remove re-registers the marketplace
tracking main and re-adds the plugin, then reports both. If that fails
too, the message gives the commands to finish by hand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(codex): don't read a marketplace table out of a multi-line string

marketplaceRef took the first line that looked like the table header,
so a `[marketplaces.postman]` example inside a multi-line string, such
as developer_instructions, hid the real table and its ref, and the
installer would re-register an explicitly pinned marketplace. It now
skips lines inside `"""` and `'''` strings, and returns undefined when
the header still appears more than once.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(codex): ask Codex for the marketplace ref instead of reading its TOML

The installer read the ref out of config.toml with a line scanner, and
each TOML form the scanner didn't model (multi-line strings, delimiters
in comments) could hide a pinned ref and get it replaced. It now asks
Codex: `config/read` over `codex app-server` returns the marketplace's
ref as Codex's own parser reads it, null when there is none. Anything
else, including an older Codex without the method, stops the install.

System gains `rpc`, which keeps the server's stdin open until the last
reply: `codex app-server` exits at end of input and drops a reply still
in flight. The smoke check reads the ref the same way.

The manual recovery commands now include `marketplace upgrade`, without
which Codex refetches at its next start and asks for approval again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(installer): ask for Codex hook consent

* fix(codex): start the manual recovery commands with the marketplace remove

When a failed migration's restore re-adds the marketplace tracking main
but can't re-add the plugin, `marketplace add --ref` is refused because
a marketplace of that name is already registered from another source.
The recovery commands now remove it first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(installer): auto-approve Codex hook

* docs: drop CONTRIBUTING changes

Keep installer documentation in README and leave the contributor guide
unchanged in this PR, as requested.

* fix(ci): run Windows installer tests in pwsh

Keep the Linux TUI skip explicit and preserve case-insensitive Windows environment keys in the isolated Codex smoke harness.

* fix(test): isolate the native Windows Codex home

Windows resolves its default home through the native profile API. Use an empty explicit CODEX_HOME there and retain the unseeded Linux install and fresh unit case.

* fix(installer): track main in Codex

Replace the release-branch dependency with approvals after installation.
Migrate existing codex-release registrations and restore them on failure.
Keep the release workflow and CONTRIBUTING changes out of the main diff.

* test(codex): decouple legacy migration fixture

Seed the legacy ref through Codex's config writer so smoke tests can run
after the remote release branch is removed.

* test(codex): bound Windows fixture write retries

commit.message:
fix(kimi): name skills as Kimi Code 2.3.0 lists them, with a fallback for older releases (#122)

* fix(kimi): name skills as Kimi Code 2.3.0 lists them, with a fallback for older releases

Kimi Code 2.3.0 lists and resolves plugin skills only as `postman:<skill>`;
2.2.0 and earlier resolve them only as `<skill>`. The Kimi mandate named
them bare, so on 2.3.0 the model's Skill("api-engineer") call failed.

The Kimi mandate is now the shared mandate, with its `postman:` names,
plus one line telling the model to drop the prefix where its skill
listing has none. The harness loads the entry skill the same way and
accepts either listing form, so validate's pinned 2.1.1 checks the bare
fallback and smoke's latest checks the prefixed names.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(kimi): accept CRLF in the Kimi mandate's naming-note check

A Windows checkout with core.autocrlf gives both mandate files CRLF, which
the LF-only suffix regex rejected, failing Installer package / Windows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(kimi): keep the shared mandate's line endings in Kimi's copy

On a CRLF checkout the inserted naming note added LF-only newlines, so a
regenerated Kimi mandate had mixed endings and differed from the file on
disk. The note now uses the shared mandate's own line ending, as the bare
rewrite it replaced did.

  lookup moved here from api-simulation, so a frontend or client consuming

  service against it, the log and faults. It gets each mock through

- Context Graph is optional. Dependencies come from the code; the owner's

  other services, or answer how it behaves when one fails; not for lookups,
  choosing an API or comparing code with a contract.
- api-mocking: a mock doesn't check what it's sent, and how to check calls
